alignment.note: Greek employs a genitive absolute construction (καταβαινόντων δὲ αὐτῶν) with the postpositive particle δέ; Latin uses a simple ablative absolute (descendentibus illis) without a connective; Syriac uses a temporal clause with ܟܕ ('when') plus active participle, all expressing the same temporal circumstance.

Greek uses the articular genitive τοῦ ὄρους ('the mountain') with preposition ἐκ; Latin mirrors this with de monte (ablative with article implied in punctuation); Syriac uses ܡܢ ܛܘܪܐ ('from the mountain') in the emphatic state, functionally equivalent but without a separate article token.

Greek διεστείλατο αὐτοῖς is aorist middle indicative with dative object; Latin præcepit illis uses active voice with dative; Syriac employs a periphrastic construction ܡܦܩܕ ܗܘܐ ܠܗܘܢ (participle + auxiliary 'was commanding to them'), reflecting Syriac preference for analytic verb forms in narrative past contexts.

Greek uses the purpose conjunction ἵνα to introduce the content clause; both Peshitta and Vulgate omit an explicit purpose marker, instead using direct construction (Syriac ܕ- relativizer, Latin ne + subjunctive), achieving the same semantic force through different syntactic means.

Greek places the relative pronoun ἃ before the verb εἶδον ('what they saw'); Vulgate follows this order (quæ vidissent); Syriac reverses to ܡܕܡ ܕܚܙܘ ('anything that they saw'), placing the indefinite substantive before the relative clause, a typical Semitic construction pattern.

Greek uses aorist subjunctive διηγήσωνται in a negative purpose clause; Latin employs present subjunctive narrarent; Syriac constructs the prohibition with ܠܐ ܢܐܡܪܘܢ ('not they should say'), using the common verb 'to say' rather than a specific 'narrate' verb, semantically equivalent in context.

The Vulgate inserts a colon after narrarent to mark the transition to the exceptive clause, a punctuation convention absent in the Greek and Syriac manuscript traditions which use no such medial stop.

Greek uses the compound exceptive εἰ μὴ ὅταν ('except when'); Latin employs nisi cum with identical force; Syriac uses ܐܠܐ ܐܢ ܡܐ (literally 'but if when'), a triple-particle construction typical of Syriac exceptive-temporal clauses, all three traditions expressing the same restrictive temporal condition.

Greek uses the articular nominative ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου with double article (before 'Son' and 'Man'); Latin Filius hominis omits articles as per Latin grammar; Syriac ܒܪܗ ܕܐܢܫܐ uses the emphatic state on both nouns with genitive particle ܕ-, functionally equivalent to the Greek articulation.

Greek ἐκ νεκρῶν uses the preposition ἐκ ('out from') with genitive plural adjective; Latin a mortuis uses ab with ablative plural; Syriac ܡܢ ܡܝܬܐ employs ܡܢ with the emphatic plural, all three expressing resurrection 'from among the dead' with tradition-specific prepositional idioms.

Greek places the aorist subjunctive ἀναστῇ at the end of the clause; Latin resurrexerit (perfect subjunctive) likewise appears clause-finally; Syriac ܕܩܡ ('that he rises') appears earlier in the clause structure, immediately after the temporal particle ܡܐ, reflecting Syriac preference for verb-initial ordering in subordinate clauses.
